fields.claim_quote:
:the [[Definition:Prime Number|primes]] of the form $4 m + 1$ are:
::$137, 139, 157$
fields.explanation: Restored missing context: the source computes primes for the n=118 range118–157. The residue-list error is independent of endpoint convention. Keep139(spurious:3mod4) and149(omitted:prime,1mod4,strictly inside range). The intended endpoint157 is below4·118/3; no theorem-level interval nonexistence is claimed. Actual Nat.Prime and Finset interval filters verify both witness facts and both open/closed enumeration variants.
fields.flaw: The proof asserts that the primes in (118, 157) of the form 4m + 1 are exactly 137, 139, 157. This enumeration is false: 139 is not of the form 4m + 1 (139 = 4*34 + 3), and 149 = 4*37 + 1, which IS of that form, is omitted. The proof also contradicts itself, having stated three lines earlier that 139 = 4 * 35 - 1.
fields.problem:
Title: Interval containing Prime Number of forms 4n - 1, 4n + 1, 6n - 1, 6n + 1

Let $n \in \Z$ be an [[Definition:Integer|integer]] such that $n \ge 118$.

Then between $n$ and $\dfrac {4 n} 3$ there exists at least one [[Definition:Prime Number|prime number]] of each of the forms:
:$4 m - 1, 4 m + 1, 6 m - 1, 6 m + 1$
fields.source_context: The list belongs to the source n=118 calculation in the range118–157, not an unrestricted list of all primes.
fields.witness:
Two independent explicit witnesses, both verified by exact integer arithmetic (deterministic trial division + the % operator; no floats).

WITNESS 1 (spurious member, interval-independent): n = 139. The proof lists 139 among "the primes of the form 4m + 1". But 139 mod 4 = 3, i.e. 139 = 4*34 + 3. Equivalently, 139 - 1 = 138 and 138 = 4*34 + 2 is not divisible by 4, so there is NO integer m with 4m + 1 = 139. (139 is indeed prime, but it lies in the residue class 3 mod 4, not 1 mod 4.) This witness needs no assumption whatsoever about the intended interval.

WITNESS 1b (the proof's own self-contradiction, mechanically confirmed): 4*35 - 1 = 139 exactly, so the proof's earlier line "139 = 4*35 - 1" places 139 in the class 4m - 1 = 4m + 3. Residue classes 1 and 3 mod 4 are disjoint, so the two lines cannot both hold; the recomputation shows 139 mod 4 = 3, so the listed-as-4m+1 line is the false one.

WITNESS 2 (omitted member): n = 149. 149 is prime (trial division to 12*12 > 149 finds no divisor) and 149 = 4*37 + 1, so 149 mod 4 = 1. Also 118 < 149 < 157, so 149 lies inside the stated range under every reading of the endpoints. It is absent from the asserted list {137, 139, 157}.

Recomputed truth: primes in 119..156 are 127, 131, 137, 139, 149, 151; those ≡ 1 (mod 4) are exactly {137, 149}. On the closed interval [118, 157] they are exactly {137, 149, 157}. Under no reading is the answer {137, 139, 157}.

Concrete "claim says X, here X = Y" form: claim says {p prime in the range : p ≡ 1 mod 4} = {137, 139, 157}; recomputed, that set = {137, 149} (open range 119..156) or {137, 149, 157} (closed range 118..157). 139 ∈ claimed set but 139 mod 4 = 3 ≠ 1; 149 ∈ true set but 149 ∉ claimed set.
